'''Melqart''' was the tutelary god of '''Tyre''' and, through Tyre's colonies, of Carthage and Gades. His name is transparent Phoenician: '''MLK + QRT''' — '''"king of the city."'''

In the Botanica venue map he is patron of '''the Dye Works''': Tyre's murex purple, and the ''melek'' root that runs through this whole corpus.

== The root ==

'''√mlk''' is among the most productive triliterals in Semitic, and unpointed Hebrew cannot distinguish its members. The same three consonants underlie ''melek'' (king), ''Milcom'' (the Ammonite god), the disputed ''Molech'', and '''Melqart'''.

Two cautions this library carries elsewhere and repeats here:

* The traditional claim that the Masoretes vocalised ''melek'' with the vowels of ''bōshet'' ("shame") to produce ''mōlek'' is '''contested''' — '''Mosca''' argued it is nineteenth-century ingenuity rather than anything the Masoretes did.
* '''Eissfeldt (1935)''', from the Carthaginian evidence, argued ''mlk'' in these passages is not a god at all but a '''type of sacrifice''' — Punic ''molk''/''mulk'' — so that the abomination is the rite, not a named deity. Dewrell has more recently called this the least problematic solution.

Say '''"the Masoretes and the ''qere/ketiv'' system"''', never "priests who lost the vowels": Hebrew is an abjad and the vowels were never written.

== Melqart is Hercules ==

The identification is ancient and explicit, not modern. '''Herodotus''' went to Tyre specifically to investigate the temple of Heracles there, and reports its priests dating the sanctuary to the city's foundation. Greek and Roman writers treat Tyrian Melqart and Heracles as the same god throughout, and the Latin form of his Gaditanian cult is '''Hercules Gaditanus''' at Gades — modern Cádiz, the western end of the Phoenician world.

That western temple is the hinge for the Institute's argument about '''Hannibal''': the oath at nine, the Alps crossing read as a deliberate reenactment of the Tenth Labour, and the shrine at Gades as the departure point. It is also why the '''Pillars of Hercules''' stand where they do — at the strait, the door of the Phoenician Atlantic.

'''Corinne Bonnet's ''Melqart''''' is the standard monograph and the place to go rather than to a summary.

== Tyrian purple ==

The dye is made from the hypobranchial gland of murex sea snails — ''Hexaplex trunculus'' and ''Bolinus brandaris'' — in quantities so small that the colour was worth more than its weight in silver and became the legal marker of rank in Rome. '''"Phoenician" itself is plausibly from Greek ''phoinix'', purple-red''': a people named for the colour they sold.

The Dye Works venue therefore has a real industry behind it, and one that ties directly to [[Punic Wax]] — the same coastline, the same craft economy, the same city.

== A caution on the wider chain ==

Melqart is regularly pulled into long identification chains — with Baal, with Ba'al Hammon, with Eshmun, with Hercules and thence with everything Herculean. The '''Heracles''' identification is on ancient record and is safe. The others vary from well-supported to speculative and should be argued individually rather than inherited from the first.
